title: Beginner To Master | Chess Speedrun | 1500 | Grandmaster Naroditsky

moves.spoken: Another game — a ten-plus-five. I want to keep hammering a narrow set of key concepts rather than sprawling across openings; the focus here isn't really theory. e4, c5.
c3 — the Alapin, preparing to build a big center with d4.
d5 is correct and in fact main-line theory.
We capture, e takes d5.
Black recaptures with the queen on d5, pulled out early — but here it's fine.
d4, challenging the center. And Black doesn't need to rush the queen away, because it's well placed for the moment.
Black takes, c takes d4.

We recapture and Black develops the knight to c6. A word of warning: people have a tendency to release the tension — if there's a trade available, they grab it — but sometimes you should resist clarifying the position.
We develop the knight to f3.
Black pins with the bishop to g4.
Here's the trick: the bishop to e2. You might think Black can just win the d4-pawn — but that's not the whole story, because the queen becomes a loosely-defended piece and White gets tactics.
Black plays e6, shoring up.
Now we reap the reward and develop the knight to c3, hitting the queen with tempo.
Black tries the bishop to b4 — it may look fancy, but it's not that good. What should White do to break the pin?
We castle — the passive bishop to d2 is unnecessary; castling is the move.
Now we can develop the light-squared bishop toward a3, and if Black doesn't castle in time, that king in the center will have a very bad time. Black plays the queen to d7.
d5, a thematic pawn thrust I played almost without calculating, dislodging the knight on c6.
Black takes on c3.
Resist the automatic recapture — consider the options. d5 takes c6, and now Black loses either his queen or his bishop.
Black trades queens on d1 and we recapture with the rook — and now two of Black's pieces are hanging at once.
Black retreats the bishop to a5, but he simply doesn't have the firepower to contain our passed pawn on the queenside.
The pawn storms forward, c takes b7, one step from queening.
Black throws the rook to b8 to blockade the pawn.
One key mistake people make is taking their foot off the gas — instead let's defend the pawn with tempo, the bishop to a6.
Black takes on f3 and we recapture with the g-pawn, and Black develops the knight to f6.
The bishop to f4 — this just wins on the spot, hitting the blockading rook.
Black plays the knight to d7 — he has to move the rook, and then we promote the pawn.
Taking on b8 with the bishop is good, no doubt — let's not overthink it, keep it simple.
Black recaptures with the knight on b8.
The rook to c1 — could you propose an alternative? This is a clear second-nature move, aiming the rook at c8.
Black shuffles the king to e7.
We plant the rook on c8, and it's goodbye — no matter what Black does.
Black tries the rook to e8, staying on the back rank.
Now something cool: the bishop to b5, continuing to harass his rook.
Black slides the rook to f8.
The rook to d7, a beautiful check.
We force the knight to take, and after we recapture the red carpet is unrolled — the pawn is about to promote.
It's simply over — nothing can stop the pawn from queening.
Let's unpack the opening: d5, e takes d5, the queen recaptures, d4.
Black took with c takes d4 — which isn't a mistake per se, if Black follows up very precisely.
We recapture with c takes d4, and the real question is whether Black can handle the resulting isolated-pawn position accurately.
And that's the ultimate error in the move order — so what should Black do instead?
Black should basically do the same thing he did.
The knight to c6 — just without releasing the tension with c takes d4.
In this version Black can play e6 or the knight to f6, and crucially White doesn't get the key knight-to-c3 with tempo.
White can try the knight to a3, angling for b5, but that's quite a bit less scary than being able to play the knight to c3.
So the move order runs c takes d4, we recapture, the knight to c6, the knight to f3.
The bishop pins on g4 — and here's an important principle: when you have an isolated pawn, it helps to know this trick.
The bishop takes on f3 — you can unpin yourself in this precise way.
We recapture and Black grabs on d4 — but the point is you don't actually lose the pawn.
Because the knight is defending the queen, we can take the knight with check, the bishop capturing on c6.
Black recaptures, and then we take on d4 — the game is over, we're up a queen.
That's the key concept — now let's get back to the speedrun.
